title: Sūrya Siddhānta
summary: The most authoritative siddhānta: a dialogue in which a being born of the Sun's portion teaches the asura Maya the motions of the planets. It gives the units of time, the yugas and the kalpa, mean and true planetary positions, eclipses, conjunctions, heliacal risings, the cosmography of the earth-globe held in space by Brahman's power, instruments, and the nine measures of time.

attribution.tradition: revealed by the Sun, through a person born of his portion, to Maya at the end of the Kṛta age (SS 1.2–9)
attribution.scholarly: anonymous; an early version was summarized by Varāhamihira (Pañcasiddhāntikā); the extant text was revised c. 800–1000 CE

tradition.text: taught at the close of the Kṛta yuga (SS 1.2)

scholarly.text: extant recension c. 8th–11th c. CE; an earlier Saura-siddhānta by the 6th c.

structure.description: 14 chapters (adhikāra), c. 500 verses: mean motions; true places; direction, place and time; lunar eclipse; solar eclipse; projection of eclipses; planetary conjunctions; conjunctions with asterisms; heliacal risings and settings; the moon's horns; the pātas; cosmography (bhūgola); instruments (jyotiṣopaniṣad); measures of time

notes: Commentaries: Raṅganātha's Gūḍhārthaprakāśa (1603), Parameśvara, Kamalākara. Local e-text: GRETIL suryasiddhanta.

title: Pañcasiddhāntikā
summary: Varāhamihira's digest of the five siddhāntas of his day — Paitāmaha, Vāsiṣṭha, Romaka, Pauliśa and Saura — preserving the otherwise lost early systems; it judges the Saura the most accurate.

title: Paitāmaha Siddhānta
summary: The siddhānta ascribed to Pitāmaha (Brahmā); its early form, close to the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa, is summarized in the Pañcasiddhāntikā; a later form is preserved in the Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa and underlies Brahmagupta's work.

title: Vāsiṣṭha Siddhānta
summary: The siddhānta ascribed to Vasiṣṭha, known from Varāhamihira's summary in the Pañcasiddhāntikā.

title: Romaka Siddhānta
summary: The 'Roman' siddhānta, known from the Pañcasiddhāntikā; the tradition later ascribes it to Romaka/Śrīṣeṇa; its name marks a western source.

title: Pauliśa Siddhānta
summary: The siddhānta of Puliśa, known from the Pañcasiddhāntikā and cited by later authors; Varāhamihira calls it accurate.

title: Āryabhaṭīya
summary: Āryabhaṭa's 121 āryā verses in four parts: the Gītikāpāda (alphabetic numerals, the kalpa and planetary revolutions), Gaṇitapāda (mathematics), Kālakriyāpāda (time-reckoning, the equal quarters of the yuga, planetary motion) and Golapāda (the sphere, the rotation of the earth, eclipses by shadow). It opens in homage to Ka, the one and many, the supreme Brahman, and closes saying its knowledge was raised from the ocean of true and false knowledge by the grace of Brahmā.

attribution.tradition: knowledge from Brahmā (Svayambhū), recovered by Āryabhaṭa at Kusumapura

tradition.text: Āryabhaṭa was 23 when 3600 years of the Kali age had passed (Kālakriyā 10)

scholarly.text: c. 499 CE (the year the text names as its author's 23rd)

structure.description: 4 pādas: Gītikā 13 (10 gīti verses + 3), Gaṇita 33, Kālakriyā 25, Gola 50 = 121 verses

notes: Local e-text with Bhāskara I's commentary (GRETIL). Correction to the unit brief: the text states the author's age at 3600 Kali (= 499 CE), not an explicit composition date.

title: Āryabhaṭasiddhānta (midnight system)
summary: Āryabhaṭa's lost second work reckoning the day from midnight (ārdharātrika), known from citations and from Brahmagupta's Khaṇḍakhādyaka and Lalla.

title: Āryabhaṭīyabhāṣya of Bhāskara I
summary: The oldest surviving prose commentary on the Āryabhaṭīya, defending Āryabhaṭa's system and explaining the origin of astronomical knowledge from Brahmā.

title: Mahābhāskarīya
summary: Bhāskara I's treatise expounding Āryabhaṭa's astronomy.

title: Laghubhāskarīya
summary: Bhāskara I's shorter manual of the Āryabhaṭa system.

title: Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta
summary: Brahmagupta's 'corrected Brāhma siddhānta', composed at Bhillamāla: astronomy, mathematics and a chapter examining other systems (tantraparīkṣā) that criticizes Āryabhaṭa for departing from the smṛti on the yugas and for teaching the rotation of the earth.

title: Khaṇḍakhādyaka
summary: Brahmagupta's handbook (karaṇa) following Āryabhaṭa's midnight system; commented by Pṛthūdaka and Āmarāja.

title: Śiṣyadhīvṛddhida
summary: Lalla's treatise 'for increasing the understanding of students', in the Āryabhaṭa school; it rejects the earth's rotation.

title: Laghumānasa
summary: Mañjula's short handbook, noted for its correction for the moon's motion.

title: Vaṭeśvarasiddhānta
summary: Vaṭeśvara's large siddhānta, defending the Āryabhaṭa school against Brahmagupta.

title: Siddhāntaśekhara
summary: Śrīpati's siddhānta of the Brāhma school.

title: Bhāsvatī
summary: Śatānanda's handbook based on the Sūrya Siddhānta, widely used in eastern India for calendar-making.

title: Siddhānta Śiromaṇi
summary: Bhāskara II's 'crest-jewel of siddhāntas' in four parts — Līlāvatī (arithmetic), Bījagaṇita (algebra), Grahagaṇita (planetary computation) and Golādhyāya (the sphere) — with his own commentary Vāsanābhāṣya. The Golādhyāya teaches that the earth rests in space by its own power without other support and has a power of attraction.

title: Līlāvatī
summary: The arithmetic of Bhāskara II, the first part of the Siddhānta Śiromaṇi; a standard school text for centuries.

title: Karaṇakutūhala
summary: Bhāskara II's handbook for calendar computation.

title: Grahalāghava
summary: Gaṇeśa Daivajña's handbook computing planetary positions without trigonometric tables; the basis of many almanacs (pañcāṅga) in western and northern India.

title: Siddhāntatattvaviveka
summary: Kamalākara's siddhānta defending the Saura school and engaging Perso-Arabic astronomy.

title: Gūḍhārthaprakāśa
summary: Raṅganātha's commentary on the Sūrya Siddhānta.

title: Grahacāranibandhana (Parahita system)
summary: Haridatta's handbook introducing the Parahita corrections to the Āryabhaṭa system in Kerala, traditionally at the Māmāṅkam festival of Tirunāvāy.

title: Dṛggaṇita
summary: Parameśvara's observation-corrected system ('computation agreeing with sight') for Kerala.

title: Goladīpikā
summary: Parameśvara's treatise on the sphere.

title: Tantrasaṅgraha
summary: Nīlakaṇṭha Somayājī's revision of planetary theory in the Saṅgamagrāma school.

title: Āryabhaṭīyabhāṣya of Nīlakaṇṭha
summary: Nīlakaṇṭha Somayājī's large commentary on the Āryabhaṭīya.

title: Yuktibhāṣā
summary: Jyeṣṭhadeva's Malayalam exposition, with demonstrations (yukti), of the mathematics and astronomy of the Tantrasaṅgraha.

title: Gaṇitasārasaṅgraha
summary: Mahāvīrācārya's Jain treatise on mathematics, opening in homage to the Jina.

title: Siddhāntadarpaṇa
summary: Sāmanta Candraśekhara's siddhānta from Odisha, built on naked-eye observation within the traditional framework.

title: Gaṇakataraṅgiṇī
summary: Sudhākara Dvivedī's Sanskrit account of the lives and works of Indian astronomers (gaṇakas).

title: Sūryaprajñapti (Sūriyapaṇṇatti)
summary: Jain canonical upāṅga on the courses of the sun, moon and asterisms in Jambūdvīpa, with the Jain doctrine of two suns and two moons and a five-year yuga close to that of the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa.

title: Candraprajñapti (Candapaṇṇatti)
summary: Jain canonical upāṅga on the moon's course, nearly identical in content to the Sūryaprajñapti.

title: Jyotiṣkaraṇḍaka (Joisakaraṇḍaga)
summary: A Jain Prakrit manual of time-reckoning and luminaries following the canonical Sūryaprajñapti.

title: Aṅgavijjā
summary: A large Jain Prakrit manual of prognostication from bodily signs, gestures and circumstances of the questioner.

title: Trailokyaprakāśa
summary: Hemaprabha's Jain Sanskrit text of Tājika and horā.

title: Śārdūlakarṇāvadāna
summary: A Buddhist avadāna (in the Divyāvadāna) in which the outcaste king Triśaṅku expounds to the brahmin Puṣkarasārin the lunar mansions, their deities and the fortunes of those born under them; an early Buddhist record of nakṣatra lore.

title: Daivajñakāmadhenu
summary: A Sanskrit manual of muhūrta and horā ascribed to the Sri Lankan monk Anavamadarśī (Saṅgharāja); evidence of jyotiṣa cultivated in a Buddhist monastic setting.

title: Vṛddhagargasaṃhitā (Gārgīya Jyotiṣa)
summary: The large early omen-compendium ascribed to the sage Garga, on lunar mansions, planets, portents and royal rites; the source Varāhamihira most often draws on for saṃhitā. Distinct from the Vaiṣṇava Garga Saṃhitā about Kṛṣṇa.

title: Yugapurāṇa
summary: The prophetic chapter of the Garga saṃhitā describing the ages and the troubles of the Kali age, including Yavana incursions.

title: Yavanajātaka
summary: Sphujidhvaja's verse rendering of a Greek horoscopic manual translated by Yavaneśvara: signs, houses, planetary natures, yogas and longevity. Scholarly account: the principal channel of Hellenistic horoscopy into India.

attribution.tradition: the teaching of the Yavanas, honoured like seers (BS 2.14)
attribution.scholarly: Pingree: prose translation 149/150 CE, versified 269/270 CE; the reading of the dates in ch. 79 is disputed by later scholars

title: Vṛddhayavanajātaka
summary: Mīnarāja's large versified horā in the Yavana tradition.

title: Bṛhajjātaka
summary: Varāhamihira's classic of horoscopy: definitions of signs, planets and houses (with Greek-derived terms), conception and birth, infant mortality, longevity (with rival teachers' methods), planetary periods, aṣṭakavarga, livelihood, royal and nābhasa yogas, lunar and two-planet yogas, the yogas for renunciation (pravrajyā), character by signs and asterisms, aspects, houses, female nativities, the manner of death and the world one goes to next, lost horoscopes and the decans. It opens by saying the horā reveals the ripening of karma earned in a former birth.

attribution.tradition: composed by Varāhamihira of Avanti, son and pupil of Ādityadāsa, who received a boon from the Sun at Kāpitthaka, after studying the views of the seers (28.9)

structure.description: 28 chapters (GRETIL numbering; Kerala editions with Rudra's Vivaraṇa count 26)

notes: Commentaries: Bhaṭṭotpala (Jagaccandrikā), Rudra (Vivaraṇa, Kerala), Govinda Bhaṭṭatiri (Daśādhyāyī on ch. 1–10).

title: Laghujātaka
summary: Varāhamihira's abridgement of his Bṛhajjātaka; its third verse compares the science to a lamp revealing the karma of past births.

title: Yogayātrā
summary: Varāhamihira's work on the timing, omens and rites of a king's military expedition, opening with a teaching that fate (karma of another birth) and human effort together bring success, and that neither favourable planets nor rites alone suffice.
notes: Local e-texts: GRETIL and Pingree's edition.

title: Ṭikkanikayātrā
summary: Varāhamihira's shorter manual of the royal expedition.

title: Vivāhapaṭala
summary: Varāhamihira's rules for the timing of marriage.

title: Bṛhat Saṃhitā
summary: Varāhamihira's encyclopaedia of mundane astrology and omens in 106 chapters: the astrologer's qualifications; the courses of sun, moon, Rāhu (with the true cause of eclipses), planets, comets, Agastya and the Seven Seers; the tortoise-division of the land; rain-forecasting; portents (utpāta) and their pacification; bodily signs; site-lore (vāstu), finding water, plants, temples, images and their consecration; animals; the marks of the five great men; gems, pearls, ruby and emerald; perfumes; augury; and the qualities of asterisms, lunar days and karaṇas for action.

structure.description: 106 chapters (Bhat/GRETIL numbering; ch. 5 Rāhucāra, 45 utpāta, 52 vāstu, 53 dakārgala, 55 prāsāda, 57 pratimā, 68 five great men, 79–82 gems, 85–95 śakuna, 97–99 asterism/tithi/karaṇa qualities, 102 marriage, 103 transits)

title: Bṛhajjātakavivaraṇa of Rudra
summary: The Kerala commentary on the Bṛhajjātaka by Rudra, edited from Trivandrum manuscripts.

title: Daśādhyāyī
summary: Govinda Bhaṭṭatiri's Kerala commentary on the first ten chapters of the Bṛhajjātaka.

title: Jagaccandrikā (Bhaṭṭotpala on the Bṛhajjātaka)
summary: Bhaṭṭotpala's commentary on the Bṛhajjātaka, the standard northern commentary.
notes: Title of the commentary from memory.

title: Bṛhat Parāśara Horā Śāstra
summary: A dialogue in which Parāśara teaches Maitreya the horā: creation from Viṣṇu and his three powers, the planets as avatāras of Janārdana who give beings the fruits of karma, planets and signs, the sixteen divisional charts, sign-aspects, the houses, special ascendants, kārakas, yogas, longevity and death-inflicting planets, a great many planetary-period systems (with the Viṃśottarī as chief), aṣṭakavarga, the five great men, renunciation yogas, curses from past births, and a long series of pacificatory rites (śānti) for planets and inauspicious births.

attribution.tradition: taught by the sage Parāśara (father of Vyāsa) to Maitreya
attribution.scholarly: a late compilation; not cited by Varāhamihira or early commentators; printed editions (19th–20th c.) vary widely in content and chapter count

tradition.text: the age of Parāśara, before the Kali age

scholarly.text: compiled in the second millennium CE; received form largely known from 19th–20th c. printed editions

structure.description: 97 chapters in the Sītārām Jhā edition (other editions differ)

notes: Local e-text used for spot checks follows the 97-chapter arrangement.

title: Laghupārāśarī (Uḍudāyapradīpa)
summary: A short text of 42 verses on the functional benefic and malefic nature of planets by house-lordship and on results of planetary periods under the Viṃśottarī system, ascribed to Parāśara's school.

title: Jaimini Upadeśa Sūtras
summary: A sūtra text in four adhyāyas of four pādas on the Jaimini system of horā: aspects by sign (rāśi-dṛṣṭi), the variable significators (cara-kāraka) headed by the ātmakāraka, the kārakāṃśa, ārūḍha and upapada, sign-based periods such as the cara-daśā, and longevity. Numbers and signs are encoded by the kaṭapayādi system. It names the signs in the chart that indicate liberation (kaivalya).

attribution.tradition: composed by the sage Jaimini (identified by the tradition with the author of the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra); held to have been composed at Kāśī
attribution.scholarly: date and authorship uncertain; attested in commentaries of the second millennium CE

scholarly.text: uncertain; first millennium CE or later

title: Sārāvalī
summary: Kalyāṇavarman's large compendium of horā drawing on Varāhamihira and the Yavanas; a principal source for later jātaka authors.

title: Horāsāra
summary: Pṛthuyaśas's summary of horā.

title: Ṣaṭpañcāśikā
summary: Pṛthuyaśas's fifty-six verses on interrogation (praśna): answering questions from the chart of the moment of asking.

title: Praśnajñāna
summary: A short interrogation text ascribed to Bhaṭṭotpala.

title: Phaladīpikā
summary: Mantreśvara's popular horā in 28 chapters: planets and signs, divisional charts, strength, yogas, houses, periods, transits (gocara), longevity and renunciation; it is a common source for the table of planetary gems.

title: Jātakapārijāta
summary: Vaidyanātha Dīkṣita's comprehensive horā in 18 chapters drawing on Varāhamihira, the Sārāvalī and Parāśara.

title: Sarvārthacintāmaṇi
summary: Veṅkaṭeśa Daivajña's horā work, much used in South India, especially on periods and house results.

title: Jātakābharaṇa
summary: Ḍhuṇḍhirāja's popular horā.

title: Jātakālaṅkāra
summary: Gaṇeśa's short versified horā.

title: Camatkāracintāmaṇi
summary: Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa's short verses on the results of planets in the houses.

title: Uttarakālāmṛta
summary: A late horā text ascribed to Kālidāsa, known for house significations and planetary kārakas.

title: Jātakapaddhati (Keśavī)
summary: Keśava Daivajña's manual of the computations for a nativity.

title: Horāratna
summary: Balabhadra's large compilation of horā.

title: Mānasāgarī
summary: An anonymous popular manual for writing horoscopes, widely used in North India.

title: Bhṛgusūtra
summary: Aphorisms ascribed to Bhṛgu on the results of planets in each house.

title: Karmavipākasaṃhitā
summary: A text relating afflictions shown by the birth-asterism quarter to specific sins of former births and prescribing expiations (a genre also found in the Purāṇas).

title: Kṛṣṇīyam
summary: A Kerala horā text used in the Nambūtiri tradition.

title: Daivajñavallabhā
summary: A text on praśna and muhūrta ascribed to Varāhamihira; the attribution is doubtful.

title: Adbhutasāgara
summary: The great digest of portents and omens begun by King Ballālasena of Bengal and completed by Lakṣmaṇasena, compiling Garga, Parāśara, Varāhamihira and the Purāṇas on celestial, atmospheric and terrestrial wonders and their pacification.

title: Vasantarāja Śākuna
summary: Vasantarāja's manual of augury from the cries and movements of birds and animals.

title: Muhūrtacintāmaṇi
summary: Rāma Daivajña's standard manual of electional timing in 13 sections: good and bad times (tithis, weekdays, their lords and classes); the asterisms and their classes; solar ingresses; transits; the sacraments (saṃskāra); marriage with the eightfold matching; the bride's entry; the second coming; establishing the fires; royal consecration; journeys; building; and entering a house.
notes: Author's own commentary Pramitākṣarā; Govinda's Pīyūṣadhārā (1603).

title: Pīyūṣadhārā
summary: Govinda's extensive commentary on the Muhūrtacintāmaṇi.

title: Muhūrtamārtaṇḍa
summary: Nārāyaṇa's manual of electional astrology.

title: Jyotiṣaratnamālā
summary: Śrīpati's influential manual of muhūrta.

title: Jyotirnibandha
summary: A digest of muhūrta and related rules compiled by Śivarāja, quoting many earlier authorities.

title: Nārada Saṃhitā (jyotiṣa)
summary: A saṃhitā on muhūrta and omens ascribed to the sage Nārada.

title: Vasiṣṭha Saṃhitā (jyotiṣa)
summary: A saṃhitā on muhūrta ascribed to Vasiṣṭha (distinct from the yoga text of the same name).

title: Kālamādhava (Kālanirṇaya)
summary: Mādhavācārya's treatise determining the right times for rites — the year, months including intercalary months, tithis and their overlaps, and festival days — combining dharmaśāstra rules with jyotiṣa reckoning.
notes: The tradition identifies Mādhavācārya with Vidyāraṇya; the identification is disputed.

title: Tājikanīlakaṇṭhī
summary: Nīlakaṇṭha's standard Tājika text in two tantras — the Saṃjñātantra (definitions: aspects, the sixteen yogas, sahamas) and the Varṣatantra (annual revolutions) — with a Praśnatantra.

title: Hāyanaratna
summary: Balabhadra's compilation on Tājika annual horoscopy.

title: Tājikaśāstra of Samarasiṃha
summary: One of the earliest Sanskrit Tājika treatises.
notes: Exact title uncertain (sometimes cited as Karmaprakāśa).

title: Praśnamārga
summary: The Kerala manual of interrogation: the conduct and qualifications of the astrologer, omens at the time of the query, the aṣṭamaṅgala and other praśna methods, diagnosis of afflictions from curses (of gods, serpents, ancestors, teachers) and spirits, and the remedies for them.

attribution.tradition: composed by a Nambūtiri of Kerala
attribution.scholarly: author's personal name not certain; dated by its own chronogram to 1649 CE

title: Nāḍī granthas (palm-leaf nāḍīs)
summary: The corpus of palm-leaf 'nāḍī' readings — Agastya, Kauśika, Bhṛgu, Śiva and other nāḍīs — which the tradition holds were written by the seers for each future consultant, organized by thumb-impression classes and chapters (kāṇḍa) on life, past births and remedies.

attribution.scholarly: manuscripts and practice largely recent and unedited

title: Bhṛgu Saṃhitā
summary: The collection of horoscope-readings ascribed to the sage Bhṛgu, held in family collections in North India, which the tradition says contains the charts of all persons.

attribution.scholarly: late manuscript collections; no critical edition

title: Candrakalā Nāḍī (Deva Keralam)
summary: A Sanskrit nāḍī text on the divisions of the signs and their results, printed in the 20th century.

title: The Holy Science (Kaivalya Darśanam)
summary: Sri Yukteswar's book harmonizing Hindu and Christian scripture, whose introduction proposes a 24,000-year cycle of four ascending and four descending yugas driven by the sun's motion around a dual star, departing from the siddhāntic figures.
